results.name: round_number_target_bonus
results.description: Among sets with no example divisible by 5, yes rate on even targets divisible by 10 minus yes rate on other even targets (pooled over trials); observed > null means people give a round-number salience bonus the model lacks, observed < null means the model over-generalises to round numbers.
results.code:
# name: round_number_target_bonus
# description: Among sets with no example divisible by 5, yes rate on even targets divisible by 10 minus yes rate on other even targets (pooled over trials); observed > null means people give a round-number salience bonus the model lacks, observed < null means the model over-generalises to round numbers.
def test_statistic(df):
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    uniq = pd.Series(sets.unique())
    ok = uniq[uniq.apply(lambda s: all(int(x) % 5 for x in s.split(",")))]
    m = sets.isin(set(ok)).values
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    ev = m & (t % 2 == 0)
    a = r[ev & (t % 10 == 0)]
    b = r[ev & (t % 10 != 0)]
    if len(a) == 0 or len(b) == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(a.mean() - b.mean())

results.name: single_example_distance_slope
results.description: For single-example sets, OLS slope of yes (per 10 units) on |target - example| over targets != example; more negative observed than null means people's generalisation from one example falls off with numeric distance more steeply than the model, less negative means flatter (more rule-like) generalisation.
results.code:
# name: single_example_distance_slope
# description: For single-example sets, OLS slope of yes (per 10 units) on |target - example| over targets != example; more negative observed than null means people's generalisation from one example falls off with numeric distance more steeply than the model, less negative means flatter (more rule-like) generalisation.
def test_statistic(df):
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    single = ~sets.str.contains(",")
    x = pd.to_numeric(sets[single], errors="coerce").values
    t = df["target"].astype(float).values[single.values]
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).values[single.values]
    keep = np.isfinite(x) & (t != x)
    d = np.abs(t[keep] - x[keep]) / 10.0
    y = r[keep]
    if len(d) < 3 or np.var(d) == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(np.cov(d, y, bias=True)[0, 1] / np.var(d))

results.name: prime_majority_exception_contrast
results.description: For sets of >=3 examples where all but one example is prime and the exception is odd (e.g. 17,11,65,53; 99,59,31,67), yes rate on non-example prime targets minus odd composite targets; observed > null means people keep a "primes" hypothesis despite the exception more than the model (which only has strays), observed < null means they abandon it for "odd" more.

results.name: odd_multiple3_rule_preference
results.description: For sets of >=2 examples that are all odd multiples of 3 (e.g. 63,27,99,33), yes rate on even multiples of 3 minus yes rate on odd non-multiples of 3 (non-example targets); observed < null means people choose "odd" over the smaller "multiples of 3" rule more than the size principle predicts, observed > null means they prefer the multiplicative rule more.
results.code:
# name: odd_multiple3_rule_preference
# description: For sets of >=2 examples that are all odd multiples of 3 (e.g. 63,27,99,33), yes rate on even multiples of 3 minus yes rate on odd non-multiples of 3 (non-example targets); observed < null means people choose "odd" over the smaller "multiples of 3" rule more than the size principle predicts, observed > null means they prefer the multiplicative rule more.
def test_statistic(df):
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str).values
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    ok = set()
    for s in pd.unique(sets):
        e = [int(x) for x in s.split(",")]
        if len(e) >= 2 and all(x % 2 == 1 and x % 3 == 0 for x in e):
            ok.add(s)
    m = np.isin(sets, list(ok))
    a = r[m & (t % 2 == 0) & (t % 3 == 0)]
    b = r[m & (t % 2 == 1) & (t % 3 != 0)]
    if len(a) == 0 or len(b) == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(a.mean() - b.mean())

results.name: set_level_yes_rate_sd
results.description: Standard deviation across example sets (with >=20 trials) of each set's overall yes rate; observed > null means people's breadth of generalisation differs more between sets (more all-or-none per set) than the model predicts, observed < null means the model's set-to-set contrasts are too extreme.

results.name: majority_parity_exception_contrast
results.description: For sets of >=3 examples where exactly one example has the other parity (e.g. 43,4,91,9), mean over sets of (yes rate on non-example targets with the majority parity minus yes rate on targets with the exception's parity); observed > null means people treat the lone odd-one-out as noise and generalise a parity rule more strongly than the model, observed < null means they honour the exception more.
results.code:
# name: majority_parity_exception_contrast
# description: For sets of >=3 examples where exactly one example has the other parity (e.g. 43,4,91,9), mean over sets of (yes rate on non-example targets with the majority parity minus yes rate on targets with the exception's parity); observed > null means people treat the lone odd-one-out as noise and generalise a parity rule more strongly than the model, observed < null means they honour the exception more.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",")
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    uniq = sets.unique()
    info = {}
    for s in uniq:
        e = [int(x) for x in s.split(",")]
        if len(e) < 3:
            continue
        odd = sum(x % 2 for x in e)
        if odd == 1:
            info[s] = (0, set(e))
        elif odd == len(e) - 1:
            info[s] = (1, set(e))
    out = []
    for s, (maj, es) in info.items():
        m = (sets.values == s)
        tt, rr = t[m], r[m]
        keep = np.array([x not in es for x in tt])
        tt, rr = tt[keep], rr[keep]
        a = rr[(tt % 2) == maj]
        b = rr[(tt % 2) != maj]
        if len(a) and len(b):
            out.append(a.mean() - b.mean())
    return float(np.mean(out)) if out else 0.0

results.name: wide_pair_offparity_inspan_yes
results.description: For two-example sets whose examples share parity and are >=30 apart (e.g. 13,91; 6,74), yes rate on targets strictly between the examples with the opposite parity; observed > null means people accept a broad magnitude range over the parity rule more than the model (beta width prior too restrictive), observed < null means less.
results.code:
# name: wide_pair_offparity_inspan_yes
# description: For two-example sets whose examples share parity and are >=30 apart (e.g. 13,91; 6,74), yes rate on targets strictly between the examples with the opposite parity; observed > null means people accept a broad magnitude range over the parity rule more than the model (beta width prior too restrictive), observed < null means less.
def test_statistic(df):
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    parts = sets.str.split(",", expand=True)
    if parts.shape[1] < 2:
        return 0.0
    two = parts.notna().sum(axis=1) == 2
    a = pd.to_numeric(parts[0], errors="coerce")
    b = pd.to_numeric(parts[1], errors="coerce")
    lo = np.minimum(a, b)
    hi = np.maximum(a, b)
    t = df["target"].astype(int)
    m = two & (a % 2 == b % 2) & ((hi - lo) >= 30) & (t > lo) & (t < hi) & (t % 2 != a % 2)
    if m.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(df["rating"][m.values].astype(float).mean())

results.name: smallest_rule_member_setsize_contrast
results.description: For multi-example sets whose smallest consistent arithmetic rule (odd/even, primes, squares, cubes, multiples of 3-12, powers of 2-10, ends in d; <=33 members) contains all examples, yes rate on non-example members of that rule for 4-example sets minus 2-example sets; observed < null means people sharpen toward the rule with more examples less than the size principle predicts, observed > null means more.
results.code:
# name: smallest_rule_member_setsize_contrast
# description: For multi-example sets whose smallest consistent arithmetic rule (odd/even, primes, squares, cubes, multiples of 3-12, powers of 2-10, ends in d; <=33 members) contains all examples, yes rate on non-example members of that rule for 4-example sets minus 2-example sets; observed < null means people sharpen toward the rule with more examples less than the size principle predicts, observed > null means more.
def test_statistic(df):
    N = range(1, 101)
    rules = [set(n for n in N if n % 2 == 1), set(range(2, 101, 2)),
             set(n for n in N if n > 1 and all(n % a for a in range(2, int(n ** 0.5) + 1))),
             set(k * k for k in range(1, 11)), set(k ** 3 for k in range(1, 5))]
    rules += [set(range(m, 101, m)) for m in [3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 11, 12]]
    rules += [set(m ** k for k in range(1, 8) if m ** k <= 100) for m in range(2, 11)]
    rules += [set(n for n in N if n % 10 == d) for d in range(10)]
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str).values
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    member = np.zeros(len(df), dtype=bool)
    nex = np.zeros(len(df), dtype=int)
    for s in pd.unique(sets):
        e = set(int(x) for x in s.split(","))
        if len(e) < 2:
            continue
        cons = [R for R in rules if e <= R and len(R) <= 33]
        if not cons:
            continue
        R = min(cons, key=len)
        m = sets == s
        mem = np.isin(t, list(R - e))
        member |= m & mem
        nex[m] = len(e)
    a = r[member & (nex == 4)]
    b = r[member & (nex == 2)]
    if len(a) == 0 or len(b) == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(a.mean() - b.mean())
